newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-CRUNCH TIME FOR AUSTRALIAN HOPEFULS.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CRUNCH TIME FOR AUSTRALIAN HOPEFULS.

text.p: The sight of Rod Laver, John Newcombe and Margaret Court back on the hallowed turf of Wimbledon on Monday was a glorious reminder of the days when Australia reigned supreme on the All England Club lawns.

For successors like Mark Philippoussis, though, living up to such legends remains a tricky business and events on the opening day suggested Pat Cash's triumph 10 years ago will remain Australia's most recent singles success for a little longer.

Philippoussis must resume on Tuesday trailing by two sets and 3-1 to Britain's Greg Rusedski, having discovered that winning the Queen's Club tournament is not necessarily a passport to immediate glory elsewhere in London.
The talented Philippoussis was identified by many over the weekend as a potential title contender and his ferocious serve will destroy dozens of opponents on grass in the years to come.

But the 20-year-old from Melbourne was not prepared for the damp, gloomy environment which greeted him on Centre Court and, unless Rusedski lets his opportunity slip when play resumes on Tuesday, the mood of Aussie optimism will be swiftly punctured.

Nevertheless Pat Rafter's achievement in reaching the French Open semifinals and Cash's brave fight through the qualifying tournament to the main draw have underlined Australian potential and there may soon be another contender alongside them.

Scott Draper, a Queenslander like Laver, will precede Rafter on Court 18 on Tuesday holding a two sets advantage over 15th seed Wayne Ferreira of South Africa with the potential to add to the good impression he has made on the ATP Tour this year.

Andre Agassi, Thomas Muster and Michael Chang have all lost to him this year, and the 23-year-old from Brisbane is one of the few overseas players in the draw who know what it feels like to succeed on grass.

He captured the Wimbledon junior doubles title in 1992 and, even from the relative depths of 66th in the world, could offer a serious threat to second seed Goran Ivanisevic if he can finish off Ferreira and advance to the last 16.
The Australian theme will also be contined on Centre Court where world number two Chang will have his grass credentials examined by Todd Woodbridge.

It could be too late for Philippoussis already but Woodbridge has a great chance to prove that the spirit of Laver, Newcombe and Court, winners of 10 Wimbledon singles titles between them in the 1960s and 1970s, is not dead yet.
